utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President. Case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. On this Monday, the 22nd of January, 2007, I'd like to say good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom, the accused, the Defence counsel, the Prosecution, and I'd like to welcome especially Mr. Pusic back to the courtroom. He's with us again. Having said that, I'm going to give the floor to the registrar for a few IC numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The OTP has submitted a list of documents to be tendered through Witness CU; that list will be Exhibit IC 230. The OTP also submitted a response to Defence exhibits tendered through Witness CU; that will be given Exhibit number IC 231. A list submitted by 2D for documents tendered through Witness CV shall be given Exhibit number IC 232. The OTP submitted a response to 3D objections regarding OTP exhibits tendered through Witness CS; that shall be given Exhibit IC 233. And 3D submitted a response -- to OTP's response to 3D's objections to the OTP list of exhibits tendered through Witness CT, that shall be given IC 234. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I understand that the Defence would like to say a few words for -- Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Being very mindful of our precious time with respect to preliminary matters or other matters, I just wish to bring to the Court's attention that we would like to schedule a 65 ter meeting with the Judges so as to not take up any courtroom time and so we can get on with the business of taking the evidence from the witnesses. The purposes with respect to the Prosecution reply that was filed on 18 January, 2007, I don't want to go into the merits of it. However, we do believe that there are a couple of matters that deserve attention. I believe it would take 15 to 20 minutes, perhaps longer, to explain; that's why I don't want to go into them. But I do believe that it's necessary for us to be heard because of a variety of issues raised by the Prosecution. Incidentally, while it's titled "Reply," it's actually a leave for reply, although the title does not suggest that. In keeping with the Court's practice, I would urge the Prosecution in future to title it properly, that is, a leave for reply and not a reply. There's one other matter, Your Honour - and I think that Mr. Murphy wanted to raise it - with regard to the atmospherics in the courtroom, and he's more prepared to address that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon. Your Honour, it's a matter of concern for the Defence - and I don't know to what extent for the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution - that there has been a considerable incidence of people feeling unwell after and during sessions in courtroom III. One incident that I need not refer to now specifically was followed on Thursday by an episode where clearly the witness felt unwell, as did three or four members of the Defence bar. In fact, if the hearing had gone on for more than another half hour or so, we might have had to leave. Your Honour, I know that Your Honour did indicate some time ago that there were concerns with the ventilation system, and we don't know to what extent that that has been remedied or is in the process of being remedied. We have made some check with counsel in the Popovic case who are experiencing many of the same problems during their time in courtroom III. So, Your Honour, we would like to suggest that further inquiries be made with a view to taking some action, because clearly, if any members of the Trial Chamber were also to become ill or members of the Prosecution, then there would be other problems, too. Your Honour, in addition to that, we do feel that it would be appropriate for proper information to be given to the accused and to others in courtroom about the extent of any medical risk that there may be. I, for one, would certainly like my medical advisors to be aware of what exactly is going on, and I would ask the Trial Chamber to consider this as an urgent matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Murphy, for intervening. As you know, last time, I asked the registrar to alert the higher authorities with respect to the ventilation of courtroom III, and the registrar has just told me that we are expecting a response tomorrow, at around 11.30. But independently of that question linked to ventilation and so on, I personally looked into the incident in the courtroom and what kind of medical implications that has, and I spoke to the Tribunal's physician a few days ago to see whether he had the necessary cardiac assistance equipment, and whether he could bring the apparatus in, as you do in aeroplanes or public places generally, to be able to provide assistance if anybody has a heart seizure. And I sent the physician a memo in that respect but have not, unfortunately, yet received an answer from him. As a few weeks have gone by, I am going to also inform, or have him inform the authorities with respect to consequences on health, because we have -- especially with regard to the audio system, because we all do listen, have our headsets on, and I'd like to see if there have been any reports, studies, conducted on the effects that sound coming in through your ears all the time might have on the brain, on the creation of tumours or anything like that. But, as I say, I haven't received a response like that, so I am waiting for specific responses or answers to those types of questions. Now, if anybody in this courtroom feels unwell, the medical -- Tribunal's assistants must come in to help, straight away, with all the instruments necessary to take blood pressure and everything else, in case of a heart attack, in case of somebody losing consciousness. It's up to the administration and the authorities to bear that in mind. Cases like that can happen, and we need medical assistance with all the equipment straight away. This causes a great deal of stress, first of all, on the witness, on everybody else, and I'm sure we all have personal experience and know very well what this stress situation can cause. So, Mr. Murphy, thank you for taking the floor and raising that issue. It will allow me, once again, to contact the administration and discuss fundamental issues like that. A few weeks ago, let me recall, there was a witness who wasn't feeling very well. He was feeling poorly, and I remember that there was nobody in the medical department to help him, to come to his aid. So once we -- if we work until 7.00 p.m., there would have to be a permanent physician or some medical staff on duty for as long as the court is in session. But, as I say, I will take all those matters up with the administration. Now, with respect to what Mr. Karnavas said and the need for a 65 ter meeting, which would take 20 minutes or so, I can but subscribe -- I cannot but subscribe to that. I agree that that would be a good idea when we have a space, a free space in between witnesses or whatever. So we're going to study that, look into the matter, so that at the earliest opportunity we can devote 20 to 30 minutes for a 65 ter meeting, to allow the Defence to intervene. So, Mr. Karnavas, rest assured that we will deal with that, and I'll let you know when those 20 or 30 minutes will be available. I think that the 65 ter meeting, as far as I'm concerned, should be held in the presence of the accused. So we can't have it in a normal sitting. And since the courtrooms are taken up with trials almost round the clock, then this meeting will have to take place and be incorporated into our schedule. But I hope we'll find 20 to 30 minutes at the earliest opportunity. Having said that, we're going to have the witness brought in to continue the testimony. We would like to have the blinds lowered for us to be able to introduce the witness. Now, as far as this particular witness is concerned, I remember that Mr. Praljak had two more questions to ask him, and the other Defence teams had some questions as well. Before I give the floor to Mr. Praljak, I myself would like to ask the witness two questions, and that perhaps will allow Mr. Praljak to see how those responses coincide with what he wants to ask him. So having given thought to the matter over the weekend, I came up with two questions that I need to ask the witness on the basis of what he testified about last week. In order to save time, I'm going to ask the registrar to have on e-court P 9517. It is the map of Mostar. May we have that brought up on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. You may be seated. I hope that you had a good weekend regardless of the storm. We're continuing your testimony, but rest assured we'll get through the cross-examination by the end of the day. I have two questions to ask you before I give the floor to Mr. Praljak, who is going to continue with his own questions. For my two questions, I need to have the map of Mostar put up on our screens. And it was P 9517. May we zoom in on that, please. Witness, we are in open session. We have the map of Mostar, and with your electronic pen, would you place a cross on the building of the bank which the sniper that you saw was located in. So could you show me where that building was, the building with the sniper. Put a cross by the building or on the building. I don't think the map is detailed enough for you to be able to localise it, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's not that it's not precise, but there are a lot of new streets. I can't make out where it is here. We have Zrinski, the Zrinski park here, and the bank is next to the park, alongside the Zrinski park. So if this is the crossroads, then it should be somewhere here, the bank building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the building housing the bank where you saw the sniper is located on the point you have just marked for us on the map. Now, with that same pen, would you give us the separation line on the 10th of May, 1993, the separation line between the HVO and the ABiH, to the best of your knowledge, if you can do that. If not, never mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This street, Aleksa Santica Street, right up to Crnica; then across Crnica, all this was the separation line, right down the Bulevar to Donja Mahala.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, the side of town where the HVO was, put a 1 for the HVO and a 2 where the BH army positions were. So 1 for HVO; 2 for ABiH.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Registrar, may we have an IC number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be given Exhibit number IC 235, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, my second question has to do with the document that had an IC number and was returned to the Prosecutor. So may we have on e-court the drawing of the Vranica building, the sketch of the Vranica building. May we have that up on our screens again, please. Mr. Mundis, do you remember the IC number, or perhaps Mr. Bos does, because the registrar cannot find this IC number. We don't have it to hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: It would have been IC 229, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] IC 229. Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, just maybe if I can assist. This was written on a hard copy paper and so there's no electronic version of this, unless it was scanned by the registry. I don't have it. It should be in the possession of the registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we can place that piece of paper on the ELMO, then, the hard copy paper. We don't seem to have it, though. The problem is that the hard copy paper -- we haven't got the hard copy paper here now. But anyway, sir, based on your recollections, you drew a sketch of the building that was divided into two, two parts of the building, and you were explaining to us that one could go from one building to the other, passing through a corridor linking the two buildings. I remember thinking back that you also drew two other buildings further up on the page, and I seem to remember seeing on that sketch a building where it said "Policije," "Police." Now, to the best of your recollection, next to the headquarters, did the police have a station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was police station number 1. Number 1 police station, that's what it was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. It was the number 1 police station. Now, to your knowledge, on the 9th of May when the attack took place, as far as you know, were there any Croats who were detained in that number 1 police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How do you mean "detained," incarcerated? They were there on duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there were duty policemen. But in that building, on the police premises, were there any prisoners, any Croatian prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. That was the only other question that I wanted to ask you. Counsel Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. Since we still see the map of Mostar on our screens, and in view of your question about the separation line on the 10th of May, 1993, I think that it would be useful in order to establish the facts or alleged facts mentioned in the indictment that we should define what the separation line was before the conflict on the 9th of May or, rather, on the 8th of May, 1993, where the separation line was on the 8th of May, 1993; in other words, to see whether that separation line shifted because of the events that took place on the 9th of May, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, when I asked you to draw in the separation line, was it the separation line before the 9th of May attack? So the day before is the 8th of May. Now, the separation line that you drew in here, is that the one that corresponds to the separation line of the 8th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The line was always there. It never moved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Praljak, you have the floor to finish up with the questions you wanted to ask this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll be brief.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: As we have the map up on our screens, I too need to use it. Could you mark in the bank building. Now, look at the corner, a little to the right and a little further up from what you indicated. The bank was a corner building and was exactly between those two streets, was it not, from this right hand -- it's a triangle. Is what I'm saying correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't do that on this map.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You will remember that the bank was a corner building with two streets running either side. So the corner to the right, opposite the park, you see the triangle opposite the park?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this where you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Was the bank between those two streets? If so, then mark it in there, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you remember that that was the bank building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a little difficult on this map, but that's the position of the bank.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The corner, the actual corner with the two streets going off it. So this first location -- so can you put the number 3, number 3 by the bank, this corner bank building where you say the sniper shot from.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want a point 3?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: No, the number 3. Number 3, please. Place a 3 on that spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Put a number 3. We can't see that that's 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is the number 3. But I don't know where else to write it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Write it further up. So this is the -- the first point that you indicated was the square, which is today called, I think, Spanish square, with the gymnasium, with the secondary school, et cetera; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, Vranica you indicated next to Crnica with a number 2, but actually it goes downwards from the square. So could you put that right? It goes from Hit towards Santiceva Street; is that correct? Is what I'm saying correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It seems that the witness is Mr. Praljak. Who answers the question that the President has put to the witness? I think we have to it take what the witness tells us and not dictate the witness what he should say and what he should mark. I do not see any value in that. It does not bring any knowledge by the witness, from the witness, to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, with all due respect, I think he's leading the witness, and he's assisting. That's what cross-examination is. You know, it's a declarative statement with an inflection, one fact at a time, in a sequential order. I believe that's what Mr. Praljak is trying to do; otherwise, it might take forever. But he is leading, and I think as long as the gentleman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Mr. Praljak would like you to indicate, maybe by number 4, the place on the map where there was the headquarters of the 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have not been leading the witness. I only asked him whether what I am saying is correct and I'm helping him. The witness can now say what I'm saying is not correct. Since two parallel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, based on the plan, can you please tell us, where was the headquarters of the 4th Corps? Where was that building? We saw its photo. You were there when you were arrested. Where was that building? Where is it on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very difficult for me to find my bearings on this map, and it is impossible for me to find it on the map.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I maybe assist the witness, Your Honours, by asking him a few additional questions, to lead him in the right direction.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Was that building maybe here where it says street of Kralj Tomislav, King Tomislav Street, the former avenue Bila Strelcevina? Do you see that upper road? Today it is called King Tomislav's road and it used to be called the avenue. Is that the avenue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the name is King Tomislav, it used to be avenue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, it was the avenue. Is it then correct that slightly below the street whose name is King Tomislav's street, and above that it says Strelcevina, so just below that there was the Vranica building.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can tell on this map, I can see the streets of King Tomislav and Stjepan Radic. I believe that somewhere here on the corner there should be that building, the building called Vranica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can you then mark that on the map.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the Vranica building should be have been here on this map.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well, then. Can you put a number 4 next to that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will have only a few more questions while I'm cross-examining. Can we have 3D 0076.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please tell me, from the Mostar hotel you were taken out by UNPROFOR; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is it correct that before you were taken out there was an order by Arif Pasalic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to give a new IC number to the map which has now been modified. There are three or four markings that have been added. Can we have the IC number for this?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number IC 236, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 3D 00676.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Before UNPROFOR came to pick you up at the Mostar Hotel, did Arif Pasalic issue an order for you to leave that hotel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: He didn't.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You have told us that, irrespective of political agreements or agreements between the leaders, that lower levels of command would not always obey command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that some negotiations were taking place in offices, but those agreements were never implemented on the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: For example, if an order came from Arif Pasalic, was that order always implemented in the way it was it issued, or were there diverging opinions by various individuals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the UNPROFOR came to take us out of the Mostar Hotel, Arif Pasalic came as well. As far as I know, and I was on the line, we had not received any orders or commands. They simply came in front of the Mostar Hotel with an APC to take us out of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In other words, Arif Pasalic, the commander of the 4th Corps, had to arrive with UNPROFOR for you to get out; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how things transpired. I only now that when we were on the front line I had seen a light, and I saw APCs in front of the hotel. And Arif Pasalic told me that the politicians agreed we had to leave the hotel.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can we now look at this document. Are you aware of the fact that in the month of April, when negotiations were taking place about the functioning of Mostar in the future, do you know that General Pellnas also participated in those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You didn't hear anything. Can we look at two items in this document. Ms. Nozica showed you a document which was a joint statement for public. This is 3D 00676.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D 00676, and it is not on e-court. Can I have it on the ELMO. It has been translated into English. I don't know why it isn't in the e-court. I have an English copy for the Judges, and while this is being placed on the ELMO -- now we have it. Why are you saying that it's not in e-court? We don't have to have it on the ELMO. It's on the e-court. Can we please look at item 1. There are two public statements. One was issued on the 20th, the other on the 21st, and they differ in their items 1, 4, and 5.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It says here -- can you please read, Witness. On the 20th of April, 1993, with the mediation of members of the UN, representatives of the HVO and ABiH met. Is it what it says here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In other words, the UNPROFOR was incorporated into the attempt to resolve the situation in Mostar. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I only know that they came to take us out of the Mostar Hotel.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can I now have item 4 on the screen, please. In item 4, it says: "The transporters of the Spanish Battalion of the UN should be placed at crossroads by the Catholic church, by the medical centre, and by the department store Hit. They will control the separation line together with the check-point command." Does it say that here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It says here, then, that the separation line already existed and how it would be controlled. Thank you very much. I have two more short questions. You said that you remained with the SIS until April; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you remain with the SIS because you believed that there would be no conflict? You stayed there until the moment you believed that there wouldn't be any conflict between the HVO and the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April it was already clear that there would not be the case, but in SIS there were people -- the deputy of Brana Kvesic came from Sarajevo; he was a Muslim, and there were a few more Muslims in the SIS. And every time I would ask them what to do, what would happen to us, and as the situation became worse, I thought that they knew better than me, because I did not have any position. Then I realised that they wanted to save their hide and nothing else, and that they did not have the correct answer. And that's when I joined the army.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: During the conflict in Mostar, before, during and after, your wife was in Split.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not my wife, my sister. She was there until 1992 when she returned.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Was it 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: She got married in 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But you told us last time that once -- at the moment when you returned to the BiH army, that your sister was in Split. How long did she stay in Split for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was in Split during the conflict with the Serbs, and she returned before the conflict between the army and the HVO started.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next Defence team, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm also going to start with the month of April, 1993, when you left SIS. Can you please tell us more precisely what the date was when you left SIS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact date, but it was between the 15th and the 17th, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you immediately go to your, as you put it, main unit, the 2nd Battalion, or did you maybe spend a few days resting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I joined my unit immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At that moment, which is the 17th of April, the latest, where was the 2nd Battalion deployed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2nd Battalion was in Vranica, Zenica, and Donja Mahala. At that time we were in the Hotel Mostar. In other words, some of the troops of the 2nd Battalion were billeted in the Mostar Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That part of the 2nd Battalion that was in the Mostar Hotel, was it there when you joined your battalion or did you come to the hotel together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was always in the Mostar Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: To the President's question about having received an order to attack the HVO, you answered that you never received such an order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive an order to defend yourselves from a possible HVO attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me -- your question put to me has to do with some paperwork. I wouldn't know anything about that. We were in the Mostar Hotel. We were there to guard it, to defend the hotel, to defend ourselves. You're asking me about some paperwork that I don't know anything about. There may have been such papers, but I wouldn't know. I was on the ground. I did not have any knowledge about that. I did not shuffle papers. I was a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's put papers aside. We'll come back to them again. Did you receive any oral order about some activities that you were supposed to undertake in order to defend yourselves from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. When we were in the hotel we were deployed in a way to be able to defend ourselves from the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at the order of your commander, Midhat Hujdur, that is, a document that was prepared by the Prosecution for your examination-in-chief. It is in the Prosecutor's bundle and the number is P 01970. Witness, could we please look at the order to see whether you're familiar with the contents of this order.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown the part of the order under 1.2, at the bottom of the document, or maybe we can show the witness the set of documents that were prepared for him as a hard copy. Maybe it will be easier for the witness to follow the text on the paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Under 1.2, Witness, it says: "The 2nd Battalion is tasked with manning defence positions in their area of responsibility. They have to close the access in the Cekrk sector, and they have to take up defence lines on the Cekrk highway, axis Semovac, Bulevar, Dr. Mujic Street -- Safet Mujic Street," if I can read this well, "the bank (new) the Vaha cafe, the dispensary of the garrison, the old hospital, the dairy, Centar II." Witness, this line that has just been mentioned and described, does it correspond completely to the separation line that you drew on the map at the request of the Presiding Judge, or does it differ from that line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It differs, but I'm not familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How does it differ? Let me put it this way: This line, as described herein as opposed to the one that you marked on the map, does it go into the area that was under the control of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer your question because I -- because I would like to answer all your questions correctly. Before the 9th of May, before the conflict, there was an invisible line, which still exists in Mostar even today. What you have read out to me has to do with the positions of the 2nd Battalion that had to be taken for defence, which is logical to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, let's move on and let's see whether you will find logic in some other things as well. It says further on in this order: "In depth of the line, block the forces of the HVO and neutralise them." And further on, could you please pay attention to the following part.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please get the B/C/S version on the screen, because the Judges have the document in the Prosecutor's bundle.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The last three lines, Witness. We're still on page 1. On the previous page. Previous page, please. At the bottom of that page, the last three lines: "Some of the troops from the 4th Company should be sent to the command of the 41st Motorised Brigade in order to reinforce the defence, to step on the Defence." Tell me, the command of the 41st Motorised Brigade was in Vranica wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, when the troops from the area of Crnica were sent to Vranica, would these troops have to go through this territory that was under the control of the HVO? This is a simple question, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the first page back on the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please look at this sentence: "Some of the troops had to start moving from their area of responsibility towards Vranica." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would they have to go through the territory under the control of the HVO in order to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could not have been under the control of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Sir, you remember where you put Vranica on the May. If you draw a diagonal line from the positions that were held by the 2nd Battalion towards Vranica, would that be at the territory under the control of the HVO or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time it was still not under the control of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It was under the control of BiH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not under anybody's control. It was no-man's land. I apologise. I was a foot soldier. Between the HVO and the BiH territories there were no bags, there were no trenches. You could move freely around the town, in inverted commas. In the evening everybody would go to their own lines, but during the day they didn't do that. During the day you could freely go to the 4th Battalion. There were no soldiers, there was nothing. And when we're talking about the period of time after we left the Mostar Hotel, it was the UNPROFOR that manned the crossroads. And everybody was free to move around the town freely.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us how come, then, on the 19th of April, 1993, your commander issued an order according to which you were supposed to reach certain lines, block HVO forces, neutralise the HVO, cross an area that was not under your control? How do you understand the order? Was it an order to take over certain territory or something else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it can't be an order to take over territory, because this is the line and we were to defend that line.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's have a look how you defended that line and look at the next sentence also on the first page. "In further action to launch an attack from the wing along the axis of Semovac, Podhum, Balinovac, and the other axis, Centar II; Rudnik. Part of the forces should be separated for taking control of Hum hill." May we have your comments on these indubitable orders for attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, let's go on to point 1.3, the next page. Unfortunately, I don't have time to look at this document in its entirety with you, so I will restrict myself to just parts of the document and the portion referring to the 2nd Battalion. In point 1.3, and this paragraph relates to the 3rd Battalion, in the middle it says, and I quote: "Part of the forces, 30 men, with weapons should be transferred to the right side and placed under the command of the commander of the 2nd Battalion." Can you explain to us whether that means that some of the men from the left bank of the Neretva River would be transferred to the right bank of the Neretva and placed under the command of the commander of your battalion? Is that what it means? Does that mean -- what we've just read out, does that mean that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know if that ever happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on. In point 1.4, it says the following: "The Nevesinje Battalion is placed under the command of the commander of the 3rd Battalion, and they will receive their assignments from him, and part of the manpower, 30 fighters with weapons, should be transferred to the right bank and deployed in the Djacki centre and economics school where they will take up their defence positions." Tell me, Witness, do you know whether these fighters of the BH army were transferred from the left bank to the right bank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, were those soldiers in fact deployed in the pupils centre, or Djacki Dom, and economics school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says that in the order, but in the pupils centre there were refugees from Gacko and Nevesinje and others, and the command of the 4th Corps was guarded from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, just part of your answer has appeared on the transcript, that there were refugees from Gacko and Nevesinje and that the command of the 4th Corps -- that the 4th Corps command was secured from that post. Can you repeat your answer again, that there were policemen there, that there were people who were armed, for the record?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were armed people there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what about the police? Were there police forces there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what forces they were, but there were soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now let's take a look at paragraph 1.6. You have it up on your screen, and it says: "The MTD," which is the mixed cannon division, "has the assignment of opening fire on targets from present positions which are given by -- targets set by," and it says "NA," the abbreviation. I'm not quite sure what "NA" stands for. Can I have some assistance? The chief of artillery, I'm told. "... of the 41st Motorised Brigade, and if the need arises, from the demands of the brigade. 82-millimetre mortars from their firing positions should open fire on targets given in the plan, the firing plan, by the chief of artillery of the 41st Motorised Brigade, as well as pursuant to requests from the battalion commander." Now, tell us, Witness, did you know of the existence of a firing plan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about artillery action, the artillery action of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I don't think there was any.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand. Wasn't what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wasn't any artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You mean there weren't any mortars or other artillery weapons or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no firing from mortars and any of the other things.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When was there no firing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. The BH army never fired until the 10th of May. That's as long as I was in the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, we'll see about that, in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I note that in the document, under number 1.6, "MTD" is explained as "motorised tank division." It doesn't make much sense, because motorised tanks -- horse-drawn tanks, I have not heard of. But you have said "mixed cannon --" "mixed cannon" something, which again is a different translation. So I think it would be helpful if we knew what actually the expression in the original refers to.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly request that the English version be placed alongside the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Trechsel, in the original the abbreviation is MTD, MTD in the original. My client, who is an expert artilleryman, told me that that was an abbreviation for mixed cannon division or gunner division. Now, with respect to the abbreviation, I think my client is right. We can ask General Petkovic if you need further explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I then -- just to -- [Microphone not activated] make the answer more specific --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I pressed the button. Would the mixture consist, in normal, below 45-degree cannons and the mortars that have the higher angle?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you're quite right. That is why it is called mixed, because it can have mortars and guns together. So that would make it mixed, with mortars and cannons. But when there is no -- when the word "mixed" isn't there, then it's just cannon. So this is mixed because it's mortar and cannons or guns conjoined into a unit which is called a division. It is not a divizija, it is a division, with two or three batteries to one division. So it might have a total of not more than 12 artillery pieces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That was quite helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I hate to intervene, but I am looking right now at the CLSS glossary dictionary that's available on the Tribunet, and they have the abbreviation "MTD" as standing for "mixed artillery battalion," which perhaps, under a more NATO terminology, might be more understandable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I can perhaps fill in by pointing out that what General Petkovic called "division" in German would be "abteilung," a part, and that's normally two or three batteries; a union below the artillery regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But if I may add, in order to avoid future discussion, Your Honours -- [Interpretation] I apologise. Maybe I should move to Croatian. To avoid any future discussion, the suggestions made by my learned colleague Mr. Mundis that we can use NATO terminology, I think, is pointless here, senseless here and in similar cases, because in other trials, many of the terminology from sentences and judgements -- a brigade, for example, when we talk about an HVO brigade or a BH army brigade, that has absolutely nothing to do with the NATO standard brigade composition. And we've seen that there is no correlation at all. So to use NATO terminology wouldn't lead to the correct understanding of the matter in hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, let's move on to the order. We come to a relatively very interesting part which concerns you, too, and that is paragraph 1.8. You have it on your screen, and it says: "The MUP of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina has the task of taking up positions and defending the old bridge and the newly built bridge at Musala, and part of the forces should launch an attack on the MUP premises of the HZ HB and the police station of Mostar, which should be taken control of and persistently defended. Try to have the Hirurgija building, surgery building, stay within our area. The manpower for launching the attack on the MUP building and police station of Mostar should be kept in readiness in Mostar Hotel." Tell us, please, Witness, you were in Hotel Mostar at the time, were you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, were you there on alert, preparing to launch an attack on the MUP building and the police station of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Why were you then, there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: To defend the hotel. Now, I apologise, but I can't understand the purpose of your questions. Judging by you, it would appear that on the 9th we attacked the HVO and not that the HVO attacked us, and that we targeted ourselves in the Vranica building. I can't understand your questions and where they're leading at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Witness. I'm going to try, like you, to understand the questions being asked. You have in front of you an order which is dated the 19th of April, 1993. Now, the order is entitled "Order for Defence." This order, which is very detailed because it goes on for a number of points, refers to an order that we don't have in front of us from the command of the 4th Corps, which seems to be linked to the general political and military situation of the Mostar municipality. And because a reliable source seems to indicate that the HVO, aided by the Croatian army, is going to attack, then this order, when you look at it, can be read in two ways: You can -- it can be interpreted as the Defence is interpreting it and saying that this is an attack that is being considered in advance. The second reading is that, following an HVO attack, this is a counter-attack. Now, the 19th of April, as counsel has just put to you, you yourself were at the Hotel Mostar. Now, if we look at paragraph 1.8, you were on standby, waiting to launch an attack on the MUP building. This is very simple now. On the 19th of April or the 20th of April, did you, in fact, attack or did you stay in the hotel? It's a very simple question. As far as you remember, what did you do, you yourself, on the 20th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were attacked at the Mostar Hotel and we defended it and us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you say at no time on the 20th of April did you launch an attack on the MUP building, as it is stated in this order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We defended ourselves. Not a single unit or company or any single man launched an attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to see clearly, last week I asked you whether your superiors had a meeting with you about a plan of attack, and your answer was to say no, there was no meeting; we received no orders, and whatever else you said. Now, there seems to be a discrepancy between this document, which does seem to be highly precise, and your position when you said that, "We were in the Mostar Hotel and that nobody asked us to attack anything or anyone," and that on the contrary, it was you who were attacked. Now, do you still maintain that position or are you changing your position now? Which is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stand by my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Now, I'd like to tell the Defence, if your hypothesis is correct, the order indicates that units are required to send in reports every two hours. So normally, if you did your work properly, you would have to look into the units and see whether reports were indeed seen out every two hours to the 41st Motorised Brigade. So if the order was executed, there should be reports, because the last paragraph of the order indicates this, says that, that the units concerned are required to send in reports every two hours. So if the order was acted upon, then the units in the field were duty-bound to report back every two hours and there must be traces of that. So I'm telling you that as a Judge. This is a question that I, as a Judge, have been asking myself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This isn't a question that I'm asking Mr. Petkovic. I don't have the right to question Mr. Petkovic. I'm asking counsel, but Mr. Petkovic spontaneously rose to his feet.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we saw the signals table attached to the order which states, on this signals chart or table, that the attack would be launched when the signal is given, and it was Rak 626. That didn't mean that the attack was on the 21st, 22nd or the 25th, but when the signal is given. So the order must be written on the same day that the attack has -- but the attack can take place in 10 days' time, once the signal is given, because it says, when you receive the signal Rak 626, you will launch the attack. And that chart is a component part of the order. That is the only way that the witness and counsel can interpret this order. That is the crux of it. So, with all the documents that we have, when the commander of the 41st Brigade says, "You receive signal Rak 626, that is when the moment of time has come for the attack to be launched." You don't have to accept my explanation, but I would like to tell you that all the documents we have, which includes the signals chart, the additional orders of the 24th for the armoured company and everything, that is a set of documents comprising this one single order. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to explain as well? When we questioned the previous witness, we handed in Arif Pasalic's order on the basis of which this particular order was made by commander Midhat Hujdur, as well as the other orders put into practice that my client referred to. The previous witness told us that he was not familiar with the document, and in view of his position in the BH army, it was not logical to ask him about any of the details contained in those documents. We now have a witness here in court who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to finish off my question. General Petkovic explained to us how this order worked, the order that was executed or went into implementation on the basis of a signal, and that we have documents with these signals. Now, in this document it says that the soldiers, you or others, must have bands on their arms, armbands of different colours. Now, to the best of your recollections, before the 9th of May, that is to say, between the 19th of April and the 9th of May, at any given time, your unit or other soldiers that you knew, were they given these armbands to put on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to what you know --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- you were a soldier. Did you know that sometimes when the troops attacked, in order to avoid confusion soldiers would be finished with bands? Did you know that or did you not know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the month of April 1993 is concerned, nobody wore any bands around their arms. We did not receive any bands.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, you have told us that the sniper war started on the 19th of April, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you please remember when this happened, at what time? Was it in the afternoon or in the morning? At least can you tell us that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the 19th of April. It was neither in the afternoon or the evening. It was on the 19th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But when during the day; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not during the day, it was during the night. That's when it all started.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Are we talking about the night between the 18th and the 19th or the night between the 19th and 20th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: We say it was on the 19th, but I don't know whether it was between the 18th and 19th, or was it on the 19th, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please try and remember whether this was the night before or the night after, because we're talking about the 19th of April at the moment.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I said that it was during the night, because it was it peaceful during the day, it means it was in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was it in the evening of the 19th, then? Very well. Can we now please look together at the same document, item 2, which is on the next page. Could we please go to item 2 or the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would kindly ask the same item to be displayed in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, could we please look at this item together. It says: "Combat readiness by 1700 hours on 19 April 1993. By that time people had to be shifted, as well as the equipment, from one bank of the river Neretva to the other bank of the Neretva River." Would that coincide with the time, with the moment, when this sniping that you mentioned started?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't see it on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Item 2, which is approximately in the middle of that page.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Readiness -- yes, I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that the English text has disappeared from the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we say that this coincides what you told us about the beginning of the sniper war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We have dealt with the separation line. Now I would like to emphasise one more thing. You remember the separation line that you marked on the map of Mostar at the request of Judge Antonetti. You remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You've told us that that separation line existed before and after the conflict on the 9th of May, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I spoke about the line in 1992, I did not mean the line between the army and the HVO. In 1992, the BH army units were in Vranica and Crnica.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking you about May 1993. Let's focus on that. I'm asking you, what was the situation like before the 9th of May and after the 9th of May? Could you please be very precise? The separation line that you drew did not change as a result of the conflict that took place on the 9th and 10th of May; in other words, the BH army managed to keep the same line as the separation line against the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now can we hear from you: When was it that you left the Hotel Mostar, and where did you go as a member of the 2nd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said it in my statement. I believe it was seven or nine days when they came to collect us, and then we went to Crnica.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You went to Crnica after the Hotel Mostar. Can you please tell us when you arrived at the logistical base, at the Kluz facility in the Vranica compound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me about the attack, I was on duty on the 8th.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I know that, but I'm not asking you that. You were very clear about that. But we don't know when was it that you arrived from Crnica in the Kluz facility.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from Crnica. We did not arrive from Crnica in the Kluz. But the military police had been established, and from Semovac we were sent to secure the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us when the military police was established?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It always existed, but in Semovac, when the troops withdrew into the barracks, that military police already existed. I don't know how else to tell you that. From there we went to secure the command, as military policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. And when was it exactly when you arrived from Crnica in the Kluz facility, to provide security there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went there every time when it was my shift.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When was it the first time that you provided security for that facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as my first shift took place. I don't know exactly when that was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when was it the first time that you had to provide security for the Kluz facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the Kluz facility. We went to the brigade and then we were deployed by the commander there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And when was the first time you provided security for the facilities in the Vranica compound? When was the first time you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that the first time you went there was on the 8th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of May, when you arrived at that facility, how many times had you been there already?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You said that you were on duty in that facility, in the logistical base, in the night between the 8th and 9th of May; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And you've also told us that you spent the night there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You've also told us that you woke up when you heard the sounds of the attack; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You've also told us that you went up to the roof of that building and that on the roof you spent the entire day together with six or seven colleagues of yours, who were also military policemen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: From the roof of that building, could you see what was going on in town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I could.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: From the roof of that building, could you also see that the HVO was trying to capture one part of the Vranica building that housed the corps command and brigade command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In addition to that, what else did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the shells were falling by our heads, we could see them shelling the left bank of the Neretva and we could see some houses ablaze.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How did the HVO attack the Vranica building? Did they attack the entire facility or just the part of the facility that housed the command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The entire facility, with the same intensity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On the following day when you descended into the cellar where the command of the corps and the brigade were, were there any civilians in the cellar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you provide the civilians with instructions as to what to do, whether to go out and surrender, or did you provide them with some other instructions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Instructions to the civilians?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The civilians were there. You knew that there was an attack going on because the HVO wanted to take the facility where the commands of the corps and the brigade were housed. You knew that the civilians were not the object of the HVO interest. Did you tell them to go out and to surrender? Was that your advice to them? Did you tell them not to put their life at risk by being in the place that was targeted by the attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but you obviously haven't a clue what the situation in Vranica was like. A fly could not go out without being hit by a bullet. Why on earth would you then suggest that I should have told the people to go out of the building? I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that all the civilians that were in the Vranica building arrived in the atomic shelter in which the command of these units were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the civilians went downstairs to the cellar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All the civilians from the Vranica building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They could not stay in their houses. They had to go downstairs to the cellar because the shells were falling and there was shooting from rifles, and nobody could leave the Vranica building, either a civilian or a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The attempt to take the Vranica building lasted for a day and somewhat longer, and you surrendered on the 10th of May.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How did the BH army defend themselves against the attack on Vranica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: How? By rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: From what positions? How many rifles? Who was shooting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that there were between 20 and 25 of us in the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The brigade command was in the atomic shelter. Are you saying you were shooting from the shelter, where you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were shooting from the area in front of the building, where the entrance to the building was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, how many soldiers were there in front of the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was nobody in front of the building. We were all in the cellar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But you have just told us that you were shooting from the area in front of the building.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, but I can't describe to you what the situation was like. It was not a military situation in which you could stand with a rifle, standing guard, firing back. You could not as much as peek to see how far the enemy had advanced because there was shooting going on. Every now and then we would fire a shot; then they would go back and then they would advance. This is how it happened. At the entrance to the building where the command was, nobody could be there because there was constant shooting, there was constant fire going on. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, was the building defended by way of opening fire on the HVO positions from some other locations, including the eastern side of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You don't know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I don't know. It is impossible. I don't think so. This was between the buildings, and whoever wanted to defend that command, they would have had to shoot at the civilians. And it is just not feasible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the BiH army, when deciding where to house the corps and brigade commands, was choosing such a location in which there was the highest number of civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You don't know that, or do you believe that this is not the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is not the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to have just one more question about your mother.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. I'll try and be quick. I haven't got many questions for you. I'd like to recapitulate some of the things that you've told us over the past few days. You already answered this question a number of times, but I'd like to broach this area. You said that in April 1993 you worked in the SIS, the S-I-S, which you call the police; is that right? I'm waiting for the interpretation. Would you repeat your answer, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in what building was SIS? Did the building have a name? Because, as we can see, buildings in Mostar tend to have names.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the commercial bank building, Privredna Banka.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: So we had SIS that you called the police. I'd like now to go back to a document shown us by the Prosecution, which you already looked at with him. It will come up on your screen. P 02146 is the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P 02146, may we have it on e-court, please. It's the Prosecution bundle, for Their Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: You will remember that it was, the document, in -- the CSB Mostar was writing to the MUP of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 30th of April, 1993. Could you tell us whether the CSB of Mostar -- security services centre, is that what it means, "CSB"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Am I correct in thinking that that is a form of secret police or special police within the Bosnia-Herzegovinian MUP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the security services centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Within MUP. But it's not the ordinary security services centre, is it, if it's the security service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know. I don't think it was anything separate or special.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Let's refresh our memories. We discussed the agreement on joint police patrols. We dealt with a portion of that, but I'd like to draw your attention to the following document. Paragraph 2 of that document, the fourth sentence from the end, which says: "In talks..." it begins with "In talks ..." and says: "In talks the representatives of the MUP HZ HB insisted that the realisation of the Vance-Owen Plan be put into operation with respect to the organisation of the police. Insistence was made on the already-established MUP organisation of the HZ HB or, rather, that the members of the MUP of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina should be incorporated into the existing organisational set-up." When we read this, then we see that this document deals with the coordination of work between the HZ HB MUP and the MUP of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Am I right in saying that? In Mostar, in April, of course.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Who, then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're not right, because we can see from this that the MUP HZ HB does not recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we wanted these organisations --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. But this was the problem raised between these two MUPs. I'm not saying who was right and who was wrong, but this deals with the problems between the two MUPs. And my question is: At the time in Mostar, we had the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the MUP of the HZ HB, and they were supposed to reach an agreement but in fact did not; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now have on e-court the following document: P 02030.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I think you have it in front of you. Yes. It is a command by Brigadier Miljenko Lasic, dated the 22nd of April, 1993, and it relates to an order in conformity with the agreement on the normalisation of relations in Mostar that we discussed at length over the past few days. So I don't want to repeat all that. Let us just look at item 5 together, as well as item 8 and item 9. Item 5, or point 5, says: "The HVO military police shall remain in the university building (the military police of the BH army shall remain in the existing facility at Semovac)." So is that along the lines of the formation that you spoke about, the formation of the military police that was at Semovac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That police was already at Semovac, but it didn't have as many men.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: But what it says here is correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now let's move on to point number 8. It says that: "Mixed teams of the military HVO police and the BH army shall be established to patrol all parts of town over a period of 24 hours and shall control the situation in town. The patrols will wear the same military uniform, without any insignia, and the patrols shall be in place until item 8 of this order is repealed." And 9: "By 1400 hours on the 22nd of April, 1993, all persons arrested by the HVO military police and the BH army shall be exchanged on the all-for-all principle." From this document it emerges that during that time, that is to say, April 1993, there was the HVO military police in existence as well as the military police of the BH army in Mostar. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Let me recapitulate. Since we've been through all this, I counted that in Mostar there was a total at the same time, that is to say, April of 1993, the military police of the HVO, the military police of the BH army, the MUP of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the MUP of the HZ HB, the SIS that you refer to as the police, the CSB which was within MUP, the MUP of BiH; in other words, six services which dealt with the security situation in Mostar and whose work -- well, attempts were made to coordinate all their work, but quite obviously this was unsuccessful; am I right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: How many of them were there, then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right in saying that there were these six branches, but you're not right in saying that the BH state had established its power and authority in Mostar, whereas the HZ HB was the illegitimate authority and that they had a parallel MUP. What you're talking about, MUP and SIS and all the rest, they were structures of the police. I don't know how that worked, but they were a parallel authority to the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't want to enter into those polemics at present. I was just interested in knowing that at the time in Mostar work had to be coordinated among the six different services in order to improve the situation in Mostar, under wartime conditions.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions, once we've established that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Any re-examination on the part of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, the Prosecution doesn't have any re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Sir, that brings your testimony to an end. Thank you for coming to The Hague and contributing to justice. We wish you, on behalf of all my colleagues, bon voyage back to your country and hope you have every success in your work. Now, before you leave the courtroom, I would like to ask Madam Usher to lower the blinds again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And may we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Flynn, you have the floor.
