utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Just as a point of information before I read the statement -- the summary, and since Your Honours touched on it, you were asking about the BiH -- the proceedings in BiH, and I mention it since it may come up at some stage in the course of these proceedings. Just to tell you that the trial chamber in BiH did, in fact, dismiss that case that you mentioned, which was against specific perpetrators, on the basis that the evidence brought before the trial chamber on that occasion was not -- was considered imprecise, incomplete, and insufficient. Notably, however, the trial chamber did make a ruling that there had been arrests, detentions, and various other crimes committed at that time on a general basis. The decision was appealed by the prosecutor to the Supreme Court of the BiH, who sent the case back for retrial with the finding that the trial chamber were incorrect in not placing sufficient reliance on the witnesses' statements. And the Supreme Court mentioned that even though there were variances in the statements, that the witnesses, for the most part, had held with previous statements given during the investigation. I thought you'd just might like to know that, in case it does come up. As regards the summary, in this case, the witness lived in West Mostar and joined the Bosnian army in April 1993. In mid-April 1993, the witness was detained, interrogated, beaten and threatened by the members of the HVO for -- [Microphone not activated] -- for several hours. The witness was again arrested on May 9, 1993, and detained in the cellar of the mechanical faculty for four days, along with other Muslims, where he saw several prisoners being beaten. Some prisoners were taken out and never returned. On the 13th of May, the witness was taken to Heliodrom where he was mistreated. After five or six days, he was released. In the period that followed, he was arrested several times by the HVO and questioned about his son. On the 7th of July, 1993, while wanting to flee to East Mostar, he was again arrested and detained for a month at the mechanical faculty building. During this period he was beaten and mistreated. The conditions were bad. The witness, on this occasion, instead of saw, which may have appeared in the 65 ter statement, he says now that the witness heard several Muslim prisoners being tortured severely. He saw Muslims were killed by the Croatian Defence Council soldiers who were kicking and beating their heads on the walls. Sometime in December 1993, the witness was shifted to Gabela where he was beaten and mistreated. After a visit of the Red Cross towards the end of December 1993, the witness was transferred back to Heliodrom and detained until March 19, 1994. During this detention, he performed forced labour at front lines of Santiceva Street in Mostar. Muslim detainees were killed while being used as human shields at the front line. HVO soldiers used to extinguish cigarettes on the backs of the prisoners who were working there. Before and after the Muslims were expelled, their houses were plundered by the HVO and their belongings removed. The witness still suffers from beatings which he received while in detention. That concludes the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to my learned friend. I would like to thank the Trial Chamber. Just one reaction. In the summary, the Prosecutor said that the witness joined, in April 1993, the Bosnian army, and this was recorded on page 15, line 8 of the record. I believe that this should be clarified and it should be said that this is the BiH army, as it indeed says in the statement, according to Rule 65 ter, and we are emphasising this because we believe that the HVO was also the Bosnian army. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Of course my colleague is correct. I was summarising by saying "Bosnian army." He joined the Armija Bosnia-Herzegovina, the BiH forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, you've heard that summary given. Did you provide written statements to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY on the 26th of May, 1997, and on the 22nd of September, 2002?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And at that time that you provided those witness statements, did you answer the questions of the investigator truthfully?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you answer those questions freely, without any coercion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And at the conclusion of both those statements, were the statements read back to you in the Bosnian language? And did you then sign the statements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you meet with the investigators again on the 26th of March, 2006, and make a correction? Did you sign that correction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: When you travelled here to The Hague, you met with an investigator and myself yesterday. Do you recall -- not yesterday, last week. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: At that point in time were you given the opportunity of reviewing your ICTY statements in the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And is it correct that you made a number of changes that my colleagues and the Defence have been notified about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I think in relation to your statement of 26th of May -- 26th of May, 1997, you wanted to correct that statement by saying that, while Mr. Anicic was present in the basement of the mechanical faculty, you did not see Mr. Anicic kick or beat the prisoners' heads on the wall. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I think you also made another short amendment to that statement of the 26th of May, 1997, where you said, at the end: "I was transferred back to Heliodrom from Gabela on either December 29th or early -- 28th or early 29th December 1993 and not December 30th," and that was on page 3, paragraph 4, of the English translation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: In the second statement of the 22nd of September, 2002, I think you made a change to say that the mechanical faculty was the headquarters of the HVO anti-terrorist unit. That was at page 3, paragraph 2, of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I think you also provided some additional information. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And you spoke about seeing Mr. Hebibovic roll down the stairs, strike against the door of your cell, which was forced open, which allowed you to look out into the hallway. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And I think you also provided the additional information that -- that you heard members of the HVO coming down the stairs, saying that they would urinate on the bodies of the two individuals who had been killed; and that when you went to clean and paint the room in which they were held later, that you saw and removed human waste from the floor and put it in sacks and that the room -- the smell of the room was quite terrible. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, you have a booklet in front of you. I would like you to turn to the front of the booklet. You'll see it, the tab. If you'd look at number 98 -- 098 -- 09806.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: The statement is under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Is this the statement which you gave to the ICTY on the 26th of May, 1997? Do you recognise the signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. We're in open session. If there's no signature, then we can stay in open session; but if there is, then we have to move into private session, Mr. Flynn.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: He's reading from a hard copy, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So do you recognise the signature at the bottom? Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And if you turn the various pages of that statement, the signature appearing at the bottom, again, is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, if you turn to the next document, document 9807. Again, is this a statement given by you to the ICTY on the 21st of September, 2002? And is that your signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And are those your initials on the following pages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: If you had to give the evidence and the content -- from those statements all over again before this Court today, would your evidence be the same as is written in those statements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, during -- in your statement of the 26th of May, 1997, at paragraph -- page 3, paragraph 4, of the English translation, you mentioned that you were transferred back to Heliodrom from Gabela at the end of December. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And I think in the original statement you said the 30th of December, but you changed that to the 28th or 29th of December. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I'd like you to have a look at document number 07378 in your booklet of documents. If you turn to the second page, you have it in Bosnian. This is a report of a prisoners-of-war shelter, basically giving the numbers of detained and released persons for the period 28th of December to the 29th of December, 1993. And if you look at the first paragraph, you have a whole list of names, and we see on the second last line the name (redacted). Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: It's just been brought to my attention that we're in open session, Your Honour. Perhaps it might be an appropriate time to go into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. I'm going to ask you two or three very short questions. I would kindly ask you not to give me long answers because I promised I would be done in a very short time. His Honour Judge Antonetti asked you about your statement, and you spoke about having seen members of the Croatian army, the Thunder and Tiger units at the Heliodrom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In your statement you say that on one occasion, while you were cleaning the area where they were, that you had a chat with one of the soldiers and that he had told you that he hailed from Travnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He hailed from Travnik, and he was a member of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I believe that everybody in the courtroom is clear on that, but let me ask you: Travnik is in Bosnia-Herzegovina, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: On that occasion, did he tell you that his family had been expelled from Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The following Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my colleague Ms. Nozica has actually dealt with my questions, but I would just like to explore one detail, to put things in a certain context. I'm talking about the HV soldier or whether he was an HV soldier in the context of these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you agree, or would you know anything about the fact that many men from Bosnia and Herzegovina before the war, before 1990, had worked in Croatia? Many of them had been employed in Croatia permanently and they would only come home on weekends or long holidays; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did that apply equally to Croats and Muslims from Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all worked, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you personally work in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. Never. This is my first trip ever out of the borders of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you have any acquaintances, friends, or relatives who worked in Croatia before 1990?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only knew some athletes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you knew that a lot of people worked in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that many of these people who worked in Croatia - and I'm referring to both Muslims and Croats - and who found themselves in Croatia in 1990 and 1991 when the aggression of the JNA started, they volunteered and they joined the National Guards, who later on became the Croatian army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You heard of such cases?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Travnik. Would you say that that would be one of such places?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would not have reason to tell me that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In your statement, on page 14, line 19 - the statement was given on the 21st of September - you mentioned an HV soldier who told you -- I apologise. It was actually earlier today that you mentioned an HVO soldier from Makarska. He told you that he hailed from Makarska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How long did you talk to him? Did you exchange two or three sentences, more or less?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he asked me why I was black and blue, I answered him and then I asked him where he was from, and then he told me, "We are from Makarska," and that was that. And then I continued digging trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: From the few words that he uttered, could you tell by his dialect, by his accent, by his way of speech, that maybe he also was from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He didn't use our dialect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It didn't sound to you like your dialect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, but Mr. Praljak does.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, do you know that the Tigers are the best-known Croatian brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they are best known, but I know that they were together with the Thunders.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: On their sleeves, did they have a number 1?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know about number 1. I did not have a closer look.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You said that you often saw them there when you were cleaning the rooms. Did the Thunders have a number 2 on their sleeves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know that on one occasion when I was taken out to be taken for forced labour they were standing behind us, and then I heard their comment and it was something to that effect: "What if these people turned against us?"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me, please, how many men, how many soldiers, did you see who might have wore the Tiger insignia? How many did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number. There was the first building that was full with Tigers. The second was full with Thunders. I don't know how many were there. I never counted heads. I'm not that type of person. I'm not the one to look how many people there were. There were many, in any case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Try and remember. When you see them in a group, you say that you saw them in their positions. How many did you see in one group at the most? Let's leave the buildings aside. Let's talk about groups. How many were there in one group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, if a corridor is 10 metres long and there were rooms on each side of the corridor, in every room there were two or three soldiers. I don't know how many there were altogether.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is enough. When they spoke amongst each other about the ID, identification, the HVO identifications, you mentioned that they were given addresses in Mostar. Is it true that they were given addresses in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I heard from them. Because they didn't have a clue about the names of the streets in Mostar that were on their IDs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And one more question. Do you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you please come closer to the microphones that are in front of you. Speak into the microphones.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: When was the first time when you saw these people whom you called the Tigers there and the Thunders? What month was that? What date was that when you first saw them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was brought to the Heliodrom for the second time. I was imprisoned and then I was transferred to the school, and from the school I was taken to work in those buildings.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: What month was that? Can you tell me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, believe me. I really don't know. I don't know whether you can believe me, but I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Why wouldn't I believe you? There's no reason for me not to believe that you can't remember. You obviously can't know how many soldiers did the Tiger brigade have at the time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: What about the Thunders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Thunders were stationed in Sisak or in Split?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that they were stationed in Split.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I don't have any other questions for you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Ms. Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go into private session, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: The second time you were arrested, you were arrested on the 7th of July, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And you were transferred to the mechanical engineering faculty the next day or on the 8th of July. You were in the medical school first.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the school of medicine first and then to the faculty.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: So that means one day later, which would make it the 8th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have on e-court once again, please, P 08534. It is the death certificate that we already looked at today.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Could I just interject here, Your Honours, with permission. It's relevant to the question that Judge Trechsel asked us earlier on. Over the break, we managed to locate a more legible copy of this death certificate. It's not up on e-court, unfortunately, but Mr. Registrar has a copy. It's a document that was submitted some months ago to Your Worships.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We have this certificate and the name does, indeed, appear. We can put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: So you arrived at the mechanical engineering faculty on the 8th of July, 1993. Let us now take a look at the date -- month, year, and the date of death for this individual. On the certificate, you can see it on the right-hand side. You'll see it better there. It's on the right-hand side. You have it on that overhead projector there. That's right. We have the day, the month, the year of death, and it says that this particular person died on the 6th of July, 1993. So that would be two days before you arrived at the mechanical engineering faculty.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true, because he died before my very own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: But you said you didn't know this man Hebibovic personally, but you were just told that that was his name. People who knew him allegedly told you. And you saw him, according to your testimony, this person, for the first time at the mechanical engineering faculty.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. When they were brought in --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Never mind, sir. It's all in your statement. I just have a brief question. We have two statements of yours; one is dated the 26th of May, 1997, and the other one is the later one which was taken on the 20th and 21st of September, 2002. In one it says, when you describe your stay at the mechanical engineering faculty on the second occasion, that is to say, July -- rather, in your first statement you said you were incarcerated for a month, and in the second statement you say about two months. Now, I'm interested in - and we have to wait for the interpretation - I'm interested in you telling me which of the two is correct, whether the incarceration period of one month or two-month period. Which is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly because I had lost all notion of time in the dark.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I understand you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, I didn't wish to interrupt my colleague, but I would like to say for the record, although it's gone off our screens, but at page 84, line 19, the witness's answer was "yes," and in brackets is "Mate Anicic." In answering the question, the witness just said yes. So this name "Mate Anicic" was not uttered by the witness on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Counsel Ibrisimovic, any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we said earlier on, Mr. President, that we have no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Prosecution, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: No re-examination by the Prosecution, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, that completes your testimony. I would like to thank you for coming to give testimony in The Hague at the request of the Prosecution. So on behalf of my colleagues, I would like to express our best wishes for your safe return home, and we wish you every success in your future activities. I'm going to ask Madam Usher to have the blinds lowered before she escorts you out of the courtroom. I'm now going to ask the registrar to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, in open session the Prosecution is going to read a summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, normal practice, as Your Honour will know, has been to read a Rule 65 ter summary of the evidence, but in view of the extremely sensitive nature of this witness's evidence, my proposal is to give a severely abridged version of the 65 ter description that we would ordinarily read out, inasmuch as to say that the witness is giving evidence as regards events in the Mostar area from August 1992 and through 1993 where she worked within the Northern Camp, the northern barracks, as they were known, in the Mostar area. During that time, she herself was a victim of sexual assault. As far as the summary is concerned, that will be the Prosecution's summary for the purposes of the public record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let's move back into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we look at the schedule, we can see that for tomorrow we have one witness, and I believe that you have envisaged two hours for the examination-in-chief of that witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. My colleague Mr. Scott will be dealing with the witness tomorrow. We do envisage two hours. It will probably, as is typically the case, be less time than that. I believe that time estimate was given precisely for the reason that the witness is a journalist, a broadcast journalist, and I believe we'll be showing some videotapes through that witness, which, of course, take a little bit of time. So I do hope and anticipate that we'll be able to start and finish the witness tomorrow, but I can't be more precise than that at this point in time because, as I indicated, Mr. Scott will be dealing with the witness and is still in the process of proofing him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will then resume tomorrow afternoon. This week we work in the afternoon, and tomorrow we shall be starting at quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 23rd day of January, 2007, at 2.00 p.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m.,
